title: SHORT‐TERM RETURN PREDICTABILITY AND REPETITIVE INSTITUTIONAL NET ORDER ACTIVITY
abstract: Abstract Half‐hour returns predict same‐half‐hour returns on subsequent days. We hypothesize that this is due to institutional traders who execute their parent orders over multiple days (“repetitive institutional traders”). Using a unique data set that provides masked trader identification and trader type, we find that the half‐hour net order submission activity of repetitive institutional traders is predictive of same‐half‐hour returns on subsequent days, and that this relation subsumes the return predictability at shorter intervals. Repetitive institutional traders incur lower transaction costs than their nonrepetitive counterparts, suggesting that other traders compete to provide liquidity to the anticipated order flow originating from the repetitive traders.

summary.oneLiner: Net order activity of institutional traders working orders over multiple days predicts same-half-hour returns on later days, and these traders pay lower transaction costs.
summary.overview: The paper finds that stock returns in a given half-hour of the trading day help predict returns in that same half-hour on later days. The authors suggest this happens because institutional traders execute their large parent orders over several days, which they call repetitive institutional traders. The net order submissions of these traders in a half-hour predict same-half-hour returns on later days, and this relation absorbs the predictability seen at shorter intervals. These traders also incur lower transaction costs (the costs of executing trades) than nonrepetitive traders, which the authors suggest reflects other traders competing to supply liquidity against their expected order flow.
summary.question: Is short-term return predictability linked to the order submission activity of repetitive institutional traders, who execute parent orders over multiple days, and how do their transaction costs compare with those of nonrepetitive traders?
summary.method: The abstract does not name a specific statistical technique. It relates half-hour net order submission activity of repetitive institutional traders to same-half-hour returns on subsequent days, and compares their transaction costs with those of nonrepetitive traders.
summary.data: The study uses a unique data set that provides masked trader identification and trader type. The market, sample period and number of traders are not stated in the available text.

It suggests that other traders compete to provide liquidity against the anticipated order flow of repetitive institutional traders, and that these traders bear lower transaction costs, which bears on how institutional orders are executed.
